title: A Mighty Long Way: My Journey to Justice at Little Rock Central High
author: Carlotta Walls LaNier
source: A Mighty Long Way (One World / Ballantine Books, 2009)
citation: LaNier, Carlotta Walls, with Lisa Frazier Page. A Mighty Long Way: My Journey to Justice at Little Rock Central High School. One World / Ballantine Books, 2009.

sections.heading: Signing Up for History: The Promise of Central High

epigraph.quote: I simply wanted the best education available in my hometown. I didn't set out to make history; history found me.
epigraph.attribution: —Carlotta Walls LaNier, A Mighty Long Way

paragraphs: In the spring of 1957, fourteen-year-old Carlotta Walls walked into the counselor's office at Dunbar Junior High School in Little Rock, Arkansas, and signed her name on a sheet of paper indicating her desire to attend Little Rock Central High School that fall. Following the Supreme Court's landmark 1954 ruling in Brown v. Board of Education declaring racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional, Little Rock had adopted a gradual integration plan.

To Carlotta, the decision was straightforward. Central High was a palatial yellow-brick campus offering state-of-the-art science laboratories, extensive advanced courses, and superior athletic facilities that segregated Dunbar High could not match. She could never have anticipated the maelstrom of racial animosity, state defiance, and international scrutiny that would greet her on opening day.

sections.heading: Facing the Mob and the Screaming Crowd

epigraph.quote: Standing between us and the school doors were bayonets held by the Arkansas National Guard—ordered there not to protect us, but to bar our entry.
epigraph.attribution: —Carlotta Walls LaNier, A Mighty Long Way

paragraphs: On September 4, 1957, Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus defied federal court orders, surrounding Central High with armed National Guard soldiers under orders to prevent Carlotta and eight other Black students—who would become known worldwide as the Little Rock Nine—from entering. An enraged white mob screamed obscenities, spat, and threatened violence.

For three weeks, the students were barred from their classes. Only after President Dwight D. Eisenhower federalized the Arkansas National Guard and deployed the elite 101st Airborne Division ('Screaming Eagles') did the Little Rock Nine finally enter Central High on September 25, 1957, escorted up the stone steps by paratroopers with fixed bayonets. Even then, inside the hallways, the students endured daily physical attacks, spitballs, shoved lockers, and verbal abuse with unyielding dignity.

sections.heading: Walking the Graduation Stage: Unbroken Determination

epigraph.quote: When they handed me my diploma, I knew that no mob, no governor, and no bomb could take away my dignity or my future.
epigraph.attribution: —Carlotta Walls LaNier, A Mighty Long Way

paragraphs: The resistance culminated in 'The Lost Year' of 1958–1959, when Little Rock voters, urged by Faubus, closed all four public high schools rather than integrate. Carlotta continued taking correspondence courses and returned when schools reopened in 1959. Despite having her home bombed by white supremacists in February 1960, she refused to back down.

In May 1960, Carlotta Walls walked across the stage at Quigley Stadium to receive her diploma, becoming the first African American female graduate of Little Rock Central High School. Her courage demonstrated that ordinary young people possess the extraordinary power to dismantle entrenched injustice and reshape the moral conscience of a nation.
